title: You dropped the wrong stash
summary: git stash drop prints a sha and says the entry is gone. It is not — a stash is a commit, and that commit is still in the object database. Get it back.
mental_model: Each stash entry is a commit whose first parent is where you were, second parent holds the index state, and third (with -u) holds untracked files. Dropping deletes the reflog entry, not the commits.

write.content:
def optimise(items):
    """Two hours of work, stashed and then dropped by mistake."""
    ranked = sorted(items, key=lambda i: i['cost'])
    return [i for i in ranked if i['cost'] < 100]

steps.title: Two stashes, one of them valuable
steps.why: stash@{0} is the scratch notes; stash@{1} is two hours of real work. The indices shift every time you push or drop, which is exactly how the wrong one gets deleted.
steps.expect: The optimiser code in the second entry.

steps.title: Drop the wrong one
steps.why: Meaning to remove the scratch notes, you drop stash@{1}. Read the output carefully: git prints the sha of the commit it just detached. That line is your recovery key.
steps.expect: 'Dropped stash@{1} (<sha>)' and only the scratch entry remaining.

verify.label: one stash entry left — the wrong one

steps.title: Confirm the work is not in the working tree either
steps.why: The file never existed on disk after stashing, and the entry is gone from the list. By every normal measure the work has vanished.

steps.title: Find the dropped commit
steps.why: `fsck --unreachable` lists commits nothing points at. The dropped stash is right there — it was never deleted, only unreferenced.
steps.expect: One or more unreachable commits, including the stash.

verify.label: the dropped stash commit is still in the object database

steps.title: Identify it by its message
steps.why: A stash commit's subject is the message you gave it. Printing each candidate's subject tells you instantly which unreachable commit is the one you want.
commands: sh -c 'for sha in $(git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs 2>/dev/null | grep "unreachable commit" | cut -d" " -f3); do echo "$sha $(git log -1 --format=%s $sha)"; done'

steps.title: Put it back in the stash list
steps.why: `git stash store` takes a commit and re-registers it as a stash entry. Cleaner than applying it directly, because it restores the entry rather than just the content.

actions.run: sh -c 'git stash store -m "recovered: schedule optimiser" $(for sha in $(git fsck --unreachable --no-reflogs 2>/dev/null | grep "unreachable commit" | cut -d" " -f3); do git log -1 --format="%H %s" $sha; done | grep "schedule optimiser" | cut -d" " -f1)'

steps.expect: Two entries again, the recovered one on top.

verify.label: the dropped stash is back in the list

steps.title: Restore the work and commit it
steps.why: Pop it like any stash. Then commit immediately — the whole incident happened because valuable work was sitting in a stash rather than on a branch.

verify.label: the wrongly dropped stash was recovered and committed
verify.hint: git fsck --unreachable, find the commit by message, git stash store it

verify.label: the recovery is a real commit now
the scratch stash is still there, untouched

pitfalls: `git stash clear` drops every entry at once and is the usual cause of this incident. The same recovery works, but you must identify each commit by message.
`git gc --prune=now` deletes unreachable objects. Recover first, tidy later.
Stash indices renumber on every push and drop. Always drop by inspecting `git stash show` first, never by remembered index.
A stash is not a branch and not backed up. Anything worth keeping for more than a day belongs on a branch.
cheatsheet: prints the dropped commit's sha — copy it
re-register a commit as a stash entry
apply a stash commit directly, without storing it
